Henry lays four counts against the marriages. They disobeyed the express command that forbade all intimacy with the heathen, and particularly in matrimonial contracts; they profaned the crown of their peculiarity, setting themselves level with those above whom God had dignified them; they distrusted his power to protect them and were led by carnal policy, hoping to make an interest with their neighbours, since a practical disbelief of God's all-sufficiency lies at the bottom of all the sorry shifts we make; and they exposed their children to the very sin that had once been the ruin of their church and nation. He is willing to hope they did not worship the gods of those lands, their captivity having cured them of idolatry, and takes the phrase about their abominations to mean only the imitation of the heathen in promiscuous marriages, which by degrees would lead to idolatry. Clarke is harder: the mourning that follows testified abhorrence not merely of taking strange wives but of joining them in their idolatrous abominations, and he judges the settlers who returned with Zerubbabel to have become little better than the Canaanite nations they were to keep separate from. Gill works out the arithmetic: some widowers took wives of those nations, they took them for their sons as well, and some who already had wives took heathen ones besides.

Henry notes that the guilty included many of the priests and Levites, whose office was to teach this law and in whom the crime was therefore greater, since it was a disparagement for that tribe to match outside it; and worse, the hand of the princes who should have prevented the trespass was chief in it, for princes in a trespass are charged as chief in it because of the influence of their example, and miserable is the people whose leaders debauch them. Clarke reads the same phrase as a comment on rank, that those who were the first men proved the most capital offenders, the first meaning the most illustrious. Henry adds that the information came from the right quarter: the princes who brought it had kept their integrity, and could not have accused others had they not been free from blame, while the man they brought it to was a ready scribe who could argue from the law and a king's commissioner who could awe the offenders. Those who cannot themselves reform public abuses, he observes, may still serve by informing those who can.

Delitzsch places the scene in the temple after Ezra's arrival and reads the signs precisely: tearing the upper and under garments was a token of heartfelt and grievous affliction, plucking out the hair an expression of violent wrath and moral indignation, not to be confused with the cutting of the hair in mourning, and sitting down astonished means desolate, rigid, without motion. Clarke notes that shaving the head and beard were signs of excessive grief and the plucking of hair much more so, since it must produce exquisite pain, and pictures Ezra withdrawn into some sequestered part of the temple, scarcely knowing what to do. Henry finds two griefs in it, the dishonour done to God by a people called by his name and the danger they were now in; the sins of others should be our sorrow, and sorrow for sin must be great sorrow, as for an only son. The company gathered of its own accord, nothing being said of their being sent for. Gill describes them as men who revered the word of God and trembled at the judgments they expected on transgressors, and Henry that those who tremble at God's word cannot but tremble at the sins of men. Wesley notes that the evening sacrifice was the hour when the people used to assemble, and that every one who fears God ought to strengthen the hands of those who act against vice and profaneness.
5:
Henry notes that devout people came into the courts at the evening sacrifice, and that Ezra chose to confess in their hearing so that they might be made sensible of their people's sins, which hitherto they had not noticed or had made light of: prayer may preach. He adds that the evening sacrifice was a type of the great propitiation, the Lamb who in the evening of the world was to take away sin by the sacrifice of himself, so that Ezra confesses with his hand as it were on the head of that sacrifice; Wesley reads the hour the same way. Gill notes what he rose from: the signs of heaviness, particularly sitting on the ground, or his fasting, having eaten nothing that day. Clarke takes the posture for the deepest humility, the hands spread as if to lay hold on the mercy of God. What follows, Henry observes, is not properly a prayer, since there is not a word of petition in it, but the offering up of devout affections.

Though clear of the guilt himself, Ezra says our sins and our trespass: Henry explains that he puts himself among the sinners as a member of the same community, and perhaps remembered against himself that he had stayed so long in Babylon; Wesley adds that the guilt had by now become national. Henry then follows the aggravations. The iniquities are increased over our heads, so that they are ready to perish as in deep waters, and grown up to the heavens, so provoking that like the sin of Sodom it cries to heaven for vengeance; yet let penitents remember that though their sins reach the heavens God's mercy is in the heavens. The fathers' example aggravates rather than excuses the sin, since we should have taken warning not to stumble at the same stone. The judgments aggravate it further, for they were delivered to the sword and to captivity and yet not reclaimed, brayed in the mortar and the folly not gone. Delitzsch gives the same train of thought: he scarcely dares lift up his face for shame at the greatness of their misdeeds, God having punished them from the days of their fathers by delivering them to their enemies, and having now turned his pity towards them. Clarke makes the shame concrete: God had so often pardoned them that Ezra was ashamed to come back to the throne of grace on their behalf, the genuine feeling of every reawakened backslider.

Delitzsch takes the little moment for the short interval between the release under Cyrus and the present, set against the long suffering before it; Clarke glosses the nail in his holy place as even so much ground as to fix their tent-poles in, Henry works through the rest: the fountain, which is grace from the Lord and not the merit of the kings of Persia, the streams, a remnant left and the house of God set up with its service in a constant method, and the effects, that it enlightened their eyes and was life from the dead; Wesley takes the wall for the favour of those kings, whose edicts were their security. On the command Henry notes that sin appears exceedingly sinful when compared with the law it breaks, while Wesley answers the policy: they may fancy that leagues and marriages are the way to establish them, but it will weaken and ruin them. Henry and Clarke both press the last aggravation, that the punishment was less than their iniquities deserved. Delitzsch explains that the closing appeal to God's righteousness is not a plea for pardon, since that righteousness would require extirpating a sinful nation, but a summons to the conscience of the community; Clarke instead takes righteous here to mean merciful, which is why a remnant escaped at all, adding that they had no righteousness but stood covered with their trespasses.
